prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength, and its development to 10^-18 fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B032 to B012. The Physics Prize is for the original experiment, verified, and with the right people credited. B012 meets all three conditions better than anything else on the table. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and demonstrated it. Ye took it to the 10^-18 regime and showed what many-body and spin-resolved effects mean for a clock. The result has been reproduced and compared at that level by independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST, SYRTE). It is a new door in the sense I care about: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, searches for drifting constants and ultralight dark matter, and a route to redefining the second are now measurements one can do. On the chair's novelty question, the 2005 prize honoured the comb, which is a ruler for optical frequencies, and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped ions. Neither contains the idea of interrogating thousands of neutral atoms in a lattice at a magic wavelength, with Doppler and recoil shifts removed and a large ensemble kept. The citation should name that idea and the 10^-18 performance, and should not name clocks or precision measurement in general. On whether a realised fundamental-physics result is required: I do not think so. The Prize has honoured instruments and measurements before their largest payoffs, and the 10^-18 agreement between independent clocks is itself the verified experimental result. I still think B032 is a real invention, but I could not make it work on attribution (see below), and a prize I cannot defend name by name is not one I should vote for.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a genuine concern. A reader may see a third clock prize and a metrology improvement rather than a new phenomenon, and I would not call that view unreasonable. The fundamental-physics payoff is still prospective: no variation of constants and no dark-matter signal has been seen, and the second has not been redefined. Katori and Ye are not the only people with a claim. Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams, and parallel ion-clock work, all contributed. I cannot verify the finer priority questions from memory, so external expert reports would help. I should also admit that part of the case for B012 is that it offends nobody, and Mark Pearce says the same. That is not a scientific argument, so I have tried to base my support on the experiment itself. The cost of moving is that I am setting aside an achievement in my own field, which I know best. Perhaps that is also a reason for me to be careful.

responses.point: Asked me to state what the decisive contribution of each of Rose, Haider and Krivanek was, and whether Knoll and others should weigh into the credit, before B032 is considered further.
responses.response: Fair question, and answering it is what moved me. As I understand it, Rose supplied the design theory for correcting spherical aberration, Haider and Rose with Uhlemann and Urban built and demonstrated the first corrected TEM, and Krivanek with Dellby and others realised a corrector for the STEM. Knoll is not part of this: the electron microscope itself was already honoured in 1986. The decisive point is that the TEM corrector was a four-person effort with Urban, and the trio of three names cannot include him. I have not checked the primary papers and cannot resolve the TEM/STEM priority split from memory. A committee should not award what its credited names cannot defend. On B022 I accept your argument that flat bands and correlated insulators do not depend on the pairing mechanism, but I still see the Cao omission as heavier than you do, since he led the original measurements. I would take it more seriously in a few years, when confirmation is broader.

responses.point: Asked how the committee can regard aberration correction as a discovery, noted Urban's omission, and judged the clock case stronger on credit and support.
responses.response: I accept the Urban point and it has been decisive for me. On the word discovery, the statutes also include invention, and I would still say that aberration correction is one. But the invention has to be credited correctly, and that is where it fails. I therefore agree with your conclusion for B012, though not entirely for your reason. My concern about B012 is the same one you raised: lattice clocks may look like a refinement of an earlier prize. I read the lattice idea as a new mechanism, because it solves the Doppler, recoil and ensemble problem together, and I would hold the citation to that mechanism. I also disagree somewhat with the idea that discovery has to mean a single new phenomenon. The lattice clock makes the observation of millimetre-scale redshift and many-body effects in a clock possible.

responses.point: Argues B012 is a verified measurement advance, with reproduction across independent laboratories, and that the optical clock overlaps the 2005 and 2012 prizes only partly.
responses.response: I agree with your technical account, and I have moved to your preferred configuration. In round 1 I said that safe is not the same as strongest. I now think that for a committee that must be absolutely sure of the topic and the names, the clean credit of B012 is a part of its scientific strength, not a substitute for it. On your uncertainty about whether the redefinition of the second matters for timing, I side with you: the measured 10^-18 agreement is enough. The place where I would press is wording. The citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice, so that it does not read as a general clock prize. I would not add the ion clocks, because that would blur the distinction from 2012.

responses.point: Prefers the Higgs discovery (B055) with Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee, but says B012 is the configuration he could support most readily if individual attribution at ATLAS and CMS is judged indefensible.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs is the more consequential result for physics as a whole, and I still think it is overdue. My difficulty is the one you describe: two collaborations of thousands, four credible names, and a limit of three. Your own file concedes that Della Negra's claim for CMS is as strong as the others, and the trios in the committee differ. The committee cannot be absolutely sure it has found the people who did the original work. That is why I put B012 ahead of it. If the committee asks external experts how to allocate the credit and gets a clear answer, I would be willing to look again, and I would keep B055 in mind for a future cycle.

responses.point: Prefers B018 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a distinct, mature, theory-plus-experiment case, and says he would not resist B012.
responses.response: I value B018 for the same reason I value B012: the prediction was tested in HgTe by an independent experiment. I have kept it as one of my alternatives. My reservations are the two you list yourself. First, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the host, and the HgTe experiment is the central confirmation, so leaving them out is a priority problem I cannot settle with the three names given. Second, the 3D Fu-Kane-Mele strand and the relation to the 2016 prize would need to be answered before I vote for it. I take your point that B018 appears in several members' alternatives, and that is a reason to keep it for the final ballot discussion if B012 fails. I do not think it is currently better than B012 on attribution.

responses.point: Moved to B012 first after the opening round, but says that consensus is not the same as being the most scientifically important candidate, and asks whether the committee should weigh B012 on merit.
responses.response: I agree with that caution, and I want to follow it. I have tried to separate the two in my own reasoning. On merit alone I might still lean toward the instrument invention in my own field. What B012 offers on merit, apart from consensus, is a result that independent laboratories have verified at the level of 10^-18 and an idea that is identifiable and attributable. I also take your point on IceCube. I regard B013 as a few years from a settled citation, since source identification is still thin, but I would not oppose it later. On your conflict note: your closeness to B013 does not affect a B012 vote, and I have no tie to Katori or Ye.

uncertainties: Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names for lattice-clock priority given Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and others. I rely on memory and would welcome external expert reports.
Whether the committee will accept that the magic-wavelength lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. The citation wording must carry this.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second or a first fundamental-physics result should be awaited. I lean to no.

My account of the Rose, Haider, Krivanek and Urban contributions in B032 is from memory and unchecked against primary publications. If a later review shows a clean three-name split, B032 could return in a later cycle.
Whether I judge B012 fairly given that I am setting aside my own field's candidate, and whether a moved preference of mine adds an independent signal or only follows the consensus.
statement.conflict_note: I am an electron microscopist at Chalmers and use aberration-corrected instruments, so B032 is close to my own field. I am no longer proposing it, and I list it only as an alternative. I have no co-authorship, institutional or funding tie to Katori or Ye. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson supports B012 independently, and I did not take that into account. I see no recusal need for B012. I have noted Johansson's possible recusal for superconducting-circuit candidates and Kroll's JILA-adjacent history, and neither affects the B012 names in a way I can identify.
